The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) enforces safety and health law at every mine in
the United States: coal mines, and "metal/nonmetal" mines such as gold and copper mines, stone
quarries and sand and gravel pits. Unlike OSHA, MSHA must inspect every underground mine four
times a year and every surface mine twice a year, and every mine operator and contractor must
report every injury and the hours their employees work. That makes mining one of the few
industries where we can compute injury rates for every single workplace. This notebook uses
calendar years 2000 to 2025. Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/us-msha-mine-safety/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           guess_max = 100000)
}

injury_summary <- read_module("tidy", "injury_summary.csv.gz")  # hours, injuries, by group
fatalities <- read_module("tidy", "fatalities.csv.gz")          # every death, 2000-2025
accidents <- read_module("tidy", "accidents.csv.gz")            # every report, 2015-2025
mines <- read_module("tidy", "mines.csv.gz")                    # every mine
mine_year <- read_module("tidy", "mine_year.csv.gz")            # one row per mine and year
viol_summary <- read_module("tidy", "violation_summary.csv.gz") # violations, by group
viol_standards <- read_module("tidy", "violation_standards.csv.gz")  # violations, by standard

# MSHA's rates leave out office workers, so we do too
mining <- filter(injury_summary, subunit != "Office workers at mine site")
```

MSHA expresses injury rates **per 200,000 hours worked**: the hours 100 full-time employees
work in a year (100 workers x 40 hours x 50 weeks). OSHA and BLS use the same base, so rates are
comparable with the SOII module. Two kinds of injury matter:

- **NFDL** (non-fatal, days lost): injuries that kept a miner off work or on restricted duty.
- **NDL** (no days lost): reported injuries that did not.

# Part 1. Deaths in US mines

```{r deaths}
deaths <- mining |>
  group_by(year, coal_metal) |>
  summarise(fatalities = sum(fatalities), hours = sum(hours), .groups = "drop") |>
  # Deaths per 100,000 full-time workers (one full-time worker = 2,000 hours a year)
  mutate(rate_per_100k = fatalities / hours * 2000 * 100000)

ggplot(deaths, aes(year, fatalities, fill = coal_metal)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Deaths in US mines", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", fill = NULL)

ggplot(deaths, aes(year, rate_per_100k, colour = coal_metal)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Deaths per 100,000 full-time workers", x = NULL, y = "Rate", colour = NULL)

# The deadliest events: several deaths on the same day at the same mine
fatalities |>
  count(accident_date, mine_id, operator_name, state, classification, name = "deaths") |>
  filter(deaths >= 3) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
```

**Questions**

1. How have deaths in coal mining and in metal/nonmetal mining changed since 2000? How have the
   *rates* changed?
2. Find the spikes in coal mining deaths. Look up the disasters listed in the table (for example,
   the 2006 Sago disaster and the 2010 Upper Big Branch explosion). What did they lead to?
3. The CFOI module reports a rate of about 3.5 deaths per 100,000 full-time workers for all US
   workers. How does mining compare, in recent years?

# Part 2. Injury rates

```{r rates}
rates <- mining |>
  group_by(year, coal_metal, worker_type) |>
  summarise(across(c(hours, nfdl_injuries, ndl_injuries), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(nfdl_rate = nfdl_injuries / hours * 200000,
         all_rate = (nfdl_injuries + ndl_injuries) / hours * 200000)

ggplot(rates, aes(year, nfdl_rate, colour = coal_metal, linetype = worker_type)) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Non-fatal days-lost injuries per 200,000 hours", x = NULL, y = "NFDL rate",
       colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)

rates |>
  filter(year == 2025) |>
  mutate(across(c(nfdl_rate, all_rate), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

**Questions**

1. By how much did the NFDL rate fall from 2000 to 2025 in coal and in metal/nonmetal mining?
2. Contractors report lower injury rates than mine operators' own employees. Give two possible
   explanations, one in which contractors really are safer and one in which they are not.
3. Compare the coal NFDL rate with the SOII rate for "Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas
   extraction" in the SOII module. Why might they differ?

# Part 3. Where in the mine, and which commodity?

```{r where}
recent <- filter(mining, year >= 2021, worker_type == "Operator")

recent |>
  group_by(coal_metal, subunit) |>
  summarise(across(c(hours, fatalities, nfdl_injuries), sum), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(hours > 1e6) |>
  mutate(nfdl_rate = round(nfdl_injuries / hours * 200000, 2),
         fatal_rate_per_100k = round(fatalities / hours * 2000 * 100000, 1),
         employees = round(hours / 2000)) |>
  arrange(desc(nfdl_rate))

recent |>
  filter(!is.na(commodity)) |>
  group_by(commodity) |>
  summarise(across(c(hours, fatalities, nfdl_injuries), sum)) |>
  mutate(nfdl_rate = round(nfdl_injuries / hours * 200000, 2),
         fatal_rate_per_100k = round(fatalities / hours * 2000 * 100000, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(nfdl_rate))
```

**Questions**

1. Which part of a mine has the highest injury rate? Why might underground work be more hazardous?
2. Which commodity has the highest injury rate, and which the highest fatality rate? Are they the
   same? Why might fatal and non-fatal injuries have different patterns?
3. Rates for small groups are unstable. Which rows here are based on fewer than about 2,000
   full-time workers (`employees`)? Would you trust their fatality rates?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. How miners die

MSHA classifies each accident by the circumstances that most directly led to it.

```{r how}
fatalities |>
  mutate(period = if_else(year <= 2012, "2000-2012", "2013-2025")) |>
  count(period, classification) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(desc(`2013-2025`)) |>
  head(10)

# Search the narratives
haulage <- filter(fatalities, classification == "Powered haulage", year >= 2020)
nrow(haulage)
haulage |>
  count(str_detect(str_to_lower(narrative), "seat ?belt"), name = "deaths")
set.seed(1)
haulage |> slice_sample(n = 3) |> pull(narrative)
```

**Questions**

1. What are the three most common classifications of fatal accidents? Which classifications fell
   most after 2012?
2. "Powered haulage" means trucks, loaders, conveyors and other vehicles and equipment that move
   material or people. Read three narratives. For each, name the hazard and one control (using
   the hierarchy of controls) that would have prevented the death.
3. None of the recent powered haulage narratives mentions a seat belt, although MSHA has run
   campaigns on seat belt use. Does that mean every victim was wearing one? What can a search of
   short narratives like these miss?

# Part 5. Violations and penalties

MSHA inspectors cite **standards** in Title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Part 56 covers
surface metal/nonmetal mines, Part 75 underground coal mines, and so on (see the data
dictionary). A violation is **significant and substantial (S&S)** if it is reasonably likely to
lead to a reasonably serious injury or illness.

```{r violations}
viol_standards |>
  filter(year >= 2021) |>
  group_by(standard, cfr_part_title) |>
  summarise(violations = sum(violations), ss = sum(significant_substantial), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share_ss = round(ss / violations, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(violations)) |>
  head(10)

viol_summary |>
  group_by(year, coal_metal) |>
  summarise(share_ss = sum(violations[significant_substantial %in% "Yes"]) / sum(violations),
            violations = sum(violations),
            proposed_millions = sum(proposed_penalty) / 1e6,
            paid_millions = sum(amount_paid) / 1e6, .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025))
```

**Questions**

1. Look up the five most-cited standards (search "30 CFR" and the section number). What hazard
   does each address?
2. Violations and penalties rose sharply after 2006 and then fell. Why might that be (hint: the
   MINER Act of 2006)?
3. How much of the proposed penalty is eventually paid? Why might the two differ?
4. The share of violations rated S&S fell from about a third in 2000 to under a fifth in 2025.
   Give two possible explanations.
